nameStory: This tiny jellyfish is named after Louis Agassiz's colleague who helped collect the first specimens from Massachusetts waters in 1849. The species name 'bachei' honors this early contributor to New England marine science, while 'Nemopsis' comes from Greek meaning 'thread-like appearance,' referring to its delicate tentacles.
description: Nemopsis bachei is a small, translucent jellyfish that drifts through New England's coastal waters as part of the zooplankton community. This gelatinous creature has a bell-shaped body with trailing tentacles that it uses to capture tiny prey. Like other cnidarians, it has stinging cells, though they're too weak to be felt by humans. It's unable to swim strongly against currents and instead drifts with the water, using its tentacles to snare small organisms that bump into them.

idTips.label: X-shaped gonads
idTips.description: When viewed from above, the reproductive organs form a distinctive X pattern that extends down the sides along the radial canals - this is the most reliable way to identify this species

idTips.label: Gelatinous bell
idTips.description: The body feels like soft, clear jelly and is nearly transparent, allowing you to see internal structures when held up to light

idTips.label: Trailing tentacles
idTips.description: Thin, thread-like tentacles extend from the bell margin and move gracefully through the water like delicate streamers

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Much smaller than the large moon jellies commonly seen, easily fitting in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Radial canals
idTips.description: Four faint lines radiating from the center to the edge are visible through the transparent bell, like spokes on a wheel

habitat: Found in both saltwater and brackish environments along New England's coast, from harbors and estuaries to nearshore ocean waters. Look for them drifting in the water column, often closer to the surface where they can encounter their preferred prey of small copepods.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, often found in shallow bays and protected areas.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant during warm months when zooplankton populations peak, easily spotted drifting near the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still present but numbers may decline as water temperatures drop, often pushed closer to shore by autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed in New England waters, likely moving to deeper or more southern waters during coldest months.

funFact: This little jellyfish is genetically related to the famous 'immortal jellyfish' that can reverse its aging process and theoretically live forever - though Nemopsis bachei hasn't mastered that trick itself!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young moon jellies, but remember the X: Nemopsis bachei has that distinctive X-shaped gonad pattern when viewed from above, while moon jellies have four horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs arranged in a cloverleaf pattern.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being discovered over 170 years ago right here in Massachusetts, this species has been observed only twice in recent New England surveys, making any sighting quite special for local marine biology.
compareHints: As the only Nemopsis species documented in New England waters, compare it to other small hydrozoans in the Bougainvilliidae family by looking for that characteristic X-shaped gonad pattern. Other family members typically have different arrangements of their reproductive organs and may lack the clear radial canal alignment that makes Nemopsis bachei distinctive.
